description: Surat-based team competing in the Universal Event, working together from one room all weekend. Our strengths: machine learning, backend engineering, UI/UX design and video storytelling. We're drawn to Earth-observation challenges, especially wildfire data (MODIS/VIIRS) and its impact on farming. Looking for: a remote sensing, geospatial or Earth science background, or someone who enjoys checking data for scientific validity. Committed to shipping a clear, working project.
summary:
MODIS has recorded fire hotspots since 2000. VIIRS joined in 2012 with sharper pixels and records about four times as many fire detections. Join the two raw datasets and the world seems to have +304% more fire starting in 2012, but that is the sensor changing, not the fire.

We built a model that converts every MODIS month into what VIIRS would have recorded, for every 25 km cell on Earth, so the record runs from November 2000 to this week without that artificial step. A web app shows it as a calendar for any country or any area you draw on the map: monthly hotspot counts, how unusual each month is compared to the historical median, where it burned, fire season patterns, decadal trends, and downloadable CSV data.

On years the model never saw, its error per 1 degree box is 18.2% against 20.3% for the best simple method. The +304% sensor step at 2012 drops to +2.4%. Estimates carry uncertainty ranges that hold the real value 90% of the time. We also checked the record against independent burned area maps, corrected outages across all four satellites, and tested it with three additional NASA sensors.
details:
What it does

The app gives you 26 years of fire activity anywhere on Earth in one consistent record. You search a country or draw a box on the map, pick a range of years, and it shows you a calendar of every month since November 2000. Each month is coloured by how it compares to the median for that calendar month, so you can tell at a glance if something is unusual. Click a month and the map shows where exactly it burned. There is also a fire season chart, a yearly record chart that puts the raw sensors next to the harmonized series with the uncertainty range of each estimate, and a panel that tells you how well the conversion actually works in that specific area. You can download the monthly table as CSV, the hotspot cells as CSV and the calendar as a PNG image. The URL keeps your view so you can share it with someone.

How it works

We took 489 million active fire hotspots from NASA FIRMS across the whole planet. That is MODIS Collection 6.1 from Terra and Aqua (2000 onward) and VIIRS 375 m from Suomi NPP (2012 onward) and NOAA-20 (2018 onward). After filtering for vegetation fires at nominal confidence or better, we group them into 0.25 degree cells and months. That gives us 189,999 cells across 313 months.

From the daily detection counts we find the days each satellite was down and scale up the months that lost data. We identified 90 runs of outage days across all four satellites, and they line up with NASA's published outage notices. Cells with lava or gas flares that get detected over and over (206 cells, 45 of them next to flagged volcanoes) are excluded. For the most recent months that have no fire type flag yet, we built a place based mask from older typed data that catches 92% of non-fire heat sources while only losing 1.1% of real fires.

The harmonization itself: from 2012 onward both MODIS and VIIRS were flying, so we know both counts. A gradient boosting model with a Poisson loss learns what VIIRS would have seen from what MODIS recorded. The inputs are things with a physical reason behind them: MODIS counts split by satellite and day versus night (Aqua crosses the equator at 13:30 like Suomi NPP, so it samples the same part of the daily fire cycle), fire radiative power, how the detections spread over days and pixels, counts in neighbouring cells and adjacent months, the cell's own fire climatology with the current month left out, and location. It also estimates the small fires in cells where MODIS saw nothing at all. We train on 2012 to 2019 only, before the MODIS orbits started drifting.

For the 20 months before Aqua joined (November 2000 to June 2002), a separate model uses only Terra inputs. Its estimates are tied to the main model through the years where both can run, so there is no gap.

NOAA-20 carries a VIIRS of the same design as Suomi NPP. We use it three ways: as a benchmark for how much two identical sensors actually disagree (8.6% per country and month), to fill the days Suomi NPP lost, and to carry the record forward after Suomi NPP stopped sending data on 2 November 2026.

Each estimated month gets an uncertainty range learned from how far off the model was when we hid real VIIRS data. Those ranges were too narrow at first (they only held the real value 84% of the time), so we widened them until they hold 90% of the time in a test across different time periods.

The web app is a static site. Every number is computed in the browser from compressed binary tile files totalling about 70 MB, so it runs from any hosting and does not need a server.

How we know it works

On years the model never saw, tested across 166 countries, the error per 1 degree box and month is 18.2%. The best simple method we could build (a local seasonal ratio plus the cell's usual small fires) gets 20.3%, and a plain ratio per country and calendar month gets 25.1%. Per 25 km cell on a log scale: 0.71 against 0.84 and 1.13.

Two VIIRS sensors of the same design disagree by 8.6% per country and month. That tells you how much disagreement is just normal between two good sensors looking at the same fires, and it is the scale to read our errors against. A third VIIRS on NOAA-21 confirms it: every pair of the three disagrees by the same amount.

The record passes through 2012 with a world step of just +2.4%, where the raw sensors joined step by +304%. At July 2002 where Aqua joins Terra, the step is also +2.4%.

We checked the record against ESA FireCCI51 and GFED5 burned area maps, which do not use any VIIRS data. In hotspots per square kilometre burned, the estimated years sit about 8% below the VIIRS years. In the raw joined data, they sit 77% below. That check does fail in boreal Asia and temperate North America, and we say so.

Landsat 8 and 9 with their 30 m pixels confirm fire in 80% of the record's biggest fire cells and months. GOES-16 geostationary data, which scans the Americas every 10 minutes, shows why MODIS based conversions get worse over time: Terra now crosses the equator at 08:46 local time instead of 10:32, and the daily cycle of fire predicts its declining count with a correlation of 0.97.

What we learned from getting it wrong

Our first model passed all its accuracy tests, but a separate seam test showed a step of up to +33% at 2012 in some regions. The cause was that VIIRS finds fires in places where MODIS saw nothing, and before 2012 those places simply did not exist in the table, so the model could not predict them. We rebuilt the model on the complete grid with every fire prone cell and month, zeros included.

Then we ran six independent reviews, each one given a different part of the project to try to break. They found a model input that leaked future data into the training (it made the months before Aqua about 13% too low), a bug in our data downloader that silently dropped 380,000 detections, and several claims in our writeup that were stronger than the evidence supported. We fixed the bugs and toned down the claims. Our lab notebook (EXPERIMENTS.md) records all 15 experiments including the ones that did not work out and the negative results.

Tools and software

Python with pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, PyArrow, h5py and Matplotlib for the data pipeline and model. JavaScript with React, Leaflet and Vite for the web app. Playwright for the demo screenshots. GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages for deployment. No special hardware. The model trains in about 30 minutes on 8 cores.

Why it matters

Right now if you want to know whether this month's fires are unusual somewhere, you can only compare against the VIIRS record starting in 2012. That is 14 years. With this project you get 26 years of consistent data with stated uncertainty. Emergency managers can judge whether a fire month is truly unprecedented. Scientists get one time series instead of two that disagree by a factor of four. Land managers can see when the burning season really starts and how it has shifted. And as MODIS retires in the next few years, the same approach keeps its long record usable going forward.
